lead: Holy Week’s first weekday sets two figures side by side, and both are quiet. In Isaiah a chosen servant will not break even a bruised reed. In John a woman says nothing at all, pours out a pound of perfume on the feet of Jesus, and is defended by him. On the first three weekdays of this week and again on Good Friday the Church reads the four Servant Songs of Isaiah, so that we walk toward the cross with the Servant before our eyes. Psalm 27 gives the answer of trust: “The Lord is my light and my salvation”.

r.h: A servant who will not break the bruised reed
set: Isaiah 40–55 speaks to the people of Judah in exile in Babylon in the sixth century before Christ. Many scholars speak of a prophet in the school of Isaiah, often called Second Isaiah, who announces that God will bring them home. Within these chapters are four poems about a mysterious Servant of the Lord (42:1–4; 49:1–6; 50:4–9; 52:13–53:12), named the Servant Songs by scholars since the late nineteenth century. Today’s reading is the first, with the verses that follow it.
str: vv. 1–4: God presents his servant: chosen, filled with the spirit, gentle, unwearied.
vv. 5–7: God the Creator speaks to the servant and gives him his mission: covenant, light, release.
kw: A servant in Israel could be a slave, but “servant of the Lord” is also a title of honour, given to Moses and David. Here the honour lies in belonging wholly to God.
It comes three times in vv. 1–4. It means more than a court’s verdict: it is the right order that God wants in the world. The servant establishes it without force.
A striking phrase: the servant does not only announce a covenant, he is himself given as a covenant (v. 6). Christians hear in this the Lord who says “the new covenant in my blood”.
vv: Here is my servant, whom I uphold, my chosen, in whom my soul delights;
The voice from heaven at the Baptism of Jesus echoes these words (Matthew 3:17), and CCC 536 sees there the beginning of his mission as the suffering Servant.
a bruised reed he will not break, and a dimly burning wick he will not quench;
A reed and a lamp’s wick are the weakest things in a house. Most conquerors break what is already cracked. This one protects it. Anyone who feels nearly finished can take heart from this verse.
to open the eyes that are blind, to bring out the prisoners from the dungeon,
For the exiles this meant release from Babylon. In the Gospels the blind see, and the Passion is the price of a wider release, from sin and death.
ch: Matthew 12:18–21 quotes the song directly and applies it to the gentle ministry of Jesus. The Catechism teaches that the Messiah’s characteristics are revealed above all in the Servant Songs, which proclaim the meaning of his Passion (CCC 713). The first song does not yet speak of suffering. It shows the manner of the one who will suffer: he wins without shouting, and he does not grow faint (v. 4) until his work is done.

set: John dates the scene “six days before the Passover”, so the countdown to the cross has begun. Bethany lies close to Jerusalem (11:18), and Lazarus, just raised from the dead, sits at the table. That raising has led the authorities to resolve on the death of Jesus (11:47–53). So life and death share this supper.

Matthew 26:6–13 and Mark 14:3–9 tell of an anointing at Bethany in which an unnamed woman pours the ointment on his head. Luke 7:36–50 tells of a sinful woman in Galilee. John alone names Mary, the sister of Martha.
str: vv. 1–3: the dinner and the anointing.
vv. 9–11: the crowd comes, and the chief priests plan to kill Lazarus too.
kw: A costly perfumed oil made from a plant of the Himalayan region, brought a very long way to the Mediterranean. The Greek word beside it, pistikēs, is uncertain, though it is usually taken as “pure”.

The money box of the group (12:6; 13:29). The verb translated “steal” (ebastazen) can also simply mean “carry”; here the two meanings meet, and John’s bitter point is that he carried it and also carried it off.
A rare word, used only here and in the parallel in Mark 14:8. Its related verb comes in John 19:40, when Joseph and Nicodemus wrap his body with spices. Mary’s act looks ahead to that tomb.
vv: Mary took a pound of costly perfume made of pure nard, anointed Jesus’ feet, and wiped them with her hair. The house was filled with the fragrance of the perfume.

A Roman pound was about 325 grams, a great quantity. It was more usual to anoint a guest’s head, so to anoint the feet is an act of deep lowliness. In the next chapter Jesus himself will wash and wipe feet. St Augustine says that as the house was filled with the scent, so the world is filled with the good report of what she did (in substance).
“Why was this perfume not sold for three hundred denarii and the money given to the poor?”
A denarius was a labourer’s day wage (Matthew 20:2), so this is the wage of most of a year. The question sounds right, which is why John adds what lay behind it (12:6).
“Leave her alone. She bought it so that she might keep it for the day of my burial.
The Greek is hard to render exactly, and translations differ. The sense is clear: she has done something fitting for what is about to happen.
ch: The Church has seen in Mary of Bethany the love that does not count the cost. Her name stands in the Roman calendar: since 2021, Mary and Lazarus are honoured with Martha on 29 July, and the calendar keeps her distinct from Mary Magdalene, with whom she was long identified in the West. The chief priests’ plan (v. 10) is John’s dark irony: they would kill a man who had been raised from the dead. Verse 9’s “crowd of the Jews” is an ordinary crowd in Judea, many of whom came to believe (v. 11). The plot belongs to some of the authorities, not to a people (CCC 597).

qa: Was Jesus saying the poor do not matter?

No. “You always have the poor with you” echoes Deuteronomy 15:11, which goes on to command open-handed giving. The Catechism says that Jesus does not soften the older demands here but invites us to recognise his own presence in the poor, who are his brethren (CCC 2449). Mary’s moment was unique: he was about to die.
study: Who is the “bruised reed” near me, and how can I avoid breaking it this week?
What is my “pound of nard”, the thing I would give to the Lord without counting the cost?
